title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: A manufacturing moat in heavy components is rarely patented; it is poured in concrete ten miles from the customer's assembly gate.
epigraph.author: Industrial Supply-Chain Maxim

web_blocks.title: Go-To-Market Anatomy: Direct B2B OEM Sequencing vs. Export Distributors

web_blocks.html: Unlike consumer brands that rely on retail dealers, SSWL runs a direct business-to-business (B2B) model [2][11]. Roughly 85% to 88% of revenue goes straight to domestic and global OEMs under multi-year platform nominations. The balance moves through US/EU export distributors and selective domestic aftermarket channels [10][11]. Winning an OEM platform follows a rigid 12-to-24-month engineering cycle [2][11]. SSWL engineers join at the CAD stage, build prototype tooling, and run TUV-certified fatigue and impact tests. Plants must also pass PPAP audits before a single production wheel is billed [2].

Once SSWL wins a Share of Business (SOB) allocation—such as 53%–60% at Tata Motors, 56%–64% at Mahindra, 64%–65% at Ashok Leyland, or 32%–36% at Maruti Suzuki—its dispatch team integrates directly with the OEM's just-in-time (JIT) enterprise resource planning schedules [11]. Wheels are bulky, heavy, and expensive to haul across highways, so shipping finished rims more than 300 to 400 kilometers erodes conversion margins rapidly. That physical reality explains SSWL's multi-hub plant map across India [25].

web_blocks.title: Raw Material Pass-Through, Working Capital Cycle & DSO Mechanics

web_blocks.html: Understanding how SSWL prices its products protects you from misreading quarterly revenue swings. Both hot-rolled steel coils and A356 aluminium alloy ingots are contractually structured as pass-through costs with OEMs [16]. Steel prices reset quarterly, while aluminium prices reset on a trailing three-month average [16]. When metal prices spike, SSWL issues supplementary invoices to OEMs—lifting reported revenue without adding proportional EBITDA rupees, which optically compresses EBITDA margin percentage even though EBITDA per wheel holds steady [14][16]. Conversely, when metal prices fall, reported revenue softens while percentage margins expand optically. The cleaner gauge of operational health is EBITDA per wheel (which rose from ₹242 to ₹404 recently) rather than raw OPM percentage alone [14].

Working capital requires tight discipline in this business. In FY26, Debtor Days stood at 43, Inventory Days at 102, and Days Payable at 108 [1]. That yielded a 38-day Cash Conversion Cycle and near-zero Working Capital Days [1]. Inventory Days sit near 90–102 days because SSWL holds steel coils, aluminium ingots, and ocean-transit export containers [1][10]. Supplier credit of 95–108 days from domestic steel and aluminium mills offsets most of that inventory load [1].

The deterministic waterfall below scales every audited line from FY26 consolidated results (₹5,183 Cr sales), without mixing TTM estimates [1]. Out of every ₹100 billed, ₹90.16 goes to raw materials, power, wages, and factory overhead, leaving ₹9.84 of Operating EBITDA [1]. Depreciation (₹2.62) and interest (₹2.37) consume nearly half of operating profit. That leaves ₹4.90 before tax and ₹3.67 in Net Profit [1]. After adding back depreciation and working-capital adjustments, Operating Cash Flow reaches ₹6.41 per ₹100 of sales. Subtracting ₹3.65 in capex leaves ₹2.76 of Free Cash Flow [1].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: The Capex-vs-Cash-Flow Equation
paragraphs: Look closely at that ₹100 waterfall. SSWL's operating cash flow of ₹6.41 per ₹100 of sales is healthy for an auto-ancillary manufacturer, and it comfortably covered ₹3.65 of capex in FY26 to leave ₹2.76 of free cash flow.

Now connect that math to the newly announced ₹1,400 Cr Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar project over 60 months—roughly ₹280 Cr per year on top of maintenance and Bhuj spending. If Q2 FY27's 12.2% EBITDA margin holds across ₹7,000+ Cr of annual revenue, internal accruals can fund most of that buildout. If margins slip back to 9.8% during a slowdown, debt will rise to bridge the gap.

book_paragraphs: Unlike consumer brands that rely on thousands of retail dealers, SSWL operates an overwhelmingly direct business-to-business model. Roughly 85% to 88% of revenue goes straight to domestic and global automakers under multi-year platform awards, with the remainder moving through North American and European export distributors and selective aftermarket channels. Winning an OEM wheel contract requires a 12-to-24-month engineering qualification cycle: SSWL co-designs the rim, runs TUV-certified fatigue and impact tests, and passes plant-level audits before billing a single wheel.

Once qualified, SSWL integrates directly with each automaker's just-in-time assembly schedule. Because wheels are heavy, bulky, and expensive to haul across highways, shipping finished rims more than 300 to 400 kilometers erodes margins. That physical constraint explains SSWL's six-plant map: Dappar serves northern India's car and tractor belt; Chennai serves southern OEMs and port exports; Jamshedpur sits next to Tata Steel and Tata Motors' commercial vehicle line; Seraikela provides backward-integrated hot-rolled steel profiles; and Mehsana and Bhuj in Gujarat concentrate alloy wheel and aluminium knuckle production near western automakers and export ports.

book_subsections.title: Pass-Through Pricing and Working Capital Mechanics
paragraphs: Contractual raw-material pass-throughs govern SSWL's revenue line. Steel prices reset quarterly and aluminium prices reset on a trailing three-month average. When metal prices surge, SSWL issues supplementary invoices that inflate top-line sales without adding proportional EBITDA rupees, compressing percentage margins optically while leaving EBITDA per wheel intact. For an owner, EBITDA per wheel—which climbed from ₹242 to ₹404—is a truer measure of factory profitability than raw operating margin percentage.

Working capital is where discipline matters most. In FY26, Debtor Days stood at 43 days and Inventory Days at 102 days—elevated because SSWL carries steel coils, aluminium ingots, and ocean-transit export containers. Fortunately, Days Payable stood at 108 days, meaning raw-material suppliers finance most of the inventory float and keep the cash conversion cycle at 38 days.

book_subsections.title: Tracing ₹100 of Sales to Free Cash Flow
paragraphs: In audited FY26 (consolidated sales of ₹5,183 Cr), ₹90.16 of every ₹100 billed went to raw materials, power, wages, and factory overhead, leaving ₹9.84 of Operating EBITDA. Depreciation of ₹2.62 and finance costs of ₹2.37 consumed roughly half of operating profit, leaving ₹4.90 before tax and ₹3.67 in Net Profit. Adding back non-cash depreciation and working-capital movements produced ₹6.41 in Operating Cash Flow, and deducting ₹3.65 in capital expenditures left ₹2.76 in Free Cash Flow per ₹100 of revenue.

That cash-flow bridge frames the central capital-allocation test ahead: with ₹1,400 Cr earmarked for Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar over 60 months, SSWL needs Q2 FY27's richer 12.2% EBITDA margin to persist so internal cash generation funds the expansion without straining leverage.

Pay close attention to the working-capital hinge inside that cash-flow bridge as well. Because SSWL carries 102 days of inventory—driven by steel coils, aluminium ingots, and ocean-bound export containers—its ability to maintain a 38-day cash conversion cycle depends on securing 100-plus days of payable credit from raw-material suppliers such as Tata Steel. If domestic steel mills ever tighten credit terms during a commodity squeeze, working-capital cash would be absorbed rapidly, turning positive free cash flow negative even if factory operating margins held steady. Understanding both the factory conversion spread and the supplier-credit float is essential before you judge the durability of SSWL's cash generation.
